quote: For my illustration, I will take the least impossible impossibility that I have ever accomplished, namely the AI-Box Experiment.
content: As evidence, the AI-Box Experiment has every feature the book teaches readers to distrust. The record, disclosed at the end of this essay, is three wins in five games; the transcripts were withheld by design; the Gatekeepers were self-selected volunteers from the author's own online circles; there was no control condition and no third-party observer. What it could show at most is that one motivated, articulate human could talk some other humans into typing a sentence in a role-play. The premise it was meant to support — that humans are not secure against persuasion — has since received real evidence from controlled studies of machine persuasion: in preregistered debates, GPT-4 given basic personal information about its opponent was more persuasive than human debaters about two thirds of the time (Salvi et al., 2025). That is what a test of the claim looks like.

quote: (One of the key Rules For Doing The Impossible is that, if you can state exactly why something is impossible, you are often close to a solution.)
content: Often, stating exactly why a problem is impossible is the solution — of the negative kind. Lindemann's proof that π is transcendental (1882) ended two millennia of attempts to square the circle; Abel and Ruffini's proof ended the search for a formula for the quintic; Turing's statement of why halting is undecidable closed that question for good. The rule is true for problems that turned out to be possible, which is a sample selected on the outcome. For a book about the dangers of trying to do what cannot be done, it omits the most common result of understanding why something is impossible: learning that it is.

quote: You might even be justified in refusing to use probabilities at this point.
content: In the domain where declining to quantify has been tested, it costs accuracy. Across a million forecasts in the US intelligence community's forecasting tournaments, rounding forecasters' numerical probabilities into coarser verbal-style bins consistently degraded accuracy — even the best forecasters' judgments contained information at a finer grain than they could say where it came from (Friedman et al., 2018). The essay's excuse — a “wildly unstable” estimate — is an argument for a wide distribution, not for none. And it sits oddly in a corpus that confidently puts numbers on God, many-worlds and cryonics, and whose author later gave high public estimates of AI catastrophe.

quote: I hope this helps explain some of my attitude when people come to me with various bright suggestions for building communities of AIs to make the whole Friendly without any of the individuals being trustworthy, or proposals for keeping an AI in a box
content: Both proposals became research programmes with results. Using untrusted models to check each other and keeping them under monitored constraint is now “AI control,” evaluated by red-team experiments (Greenblatt et al., 2024); having AIs argue while a weaker judge decides is “debate” (Irving, Christiano & Amodei, 2018), and experiments find that debate between stronger models helps weaker judges reach true answers more often (Khan et al., 2024). None of this shows the problem solved. But the rule stated here — reject any proposal that involves “only an ordinary effort,” because the problem is impossible — rejects every proposal that could be tested, and protects the claim of impossibility from the only kind of evidence that could bear on it.
